screens.title: Complex Data Structures and State Management
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter we focus on real-world ledger data: nested objects, arrays, and indexed relationships. You will learn how to convert Go application structs into JSON byte arrays for safe storage on the ledger, and how to build composite keys to query by multiple attributes. We will use concrete examples such as a Car asset with service records and a Product composed of multiple components. Understanding serialization and keying is important because Fabric stores state as byte arrays and your query patterns must be encoded into your data model. A common mistake is trying to store a Go struct directly or failing to check errors when marshalling and unmarshalling; we'll show safe patterns to avoid that. By the end of this lesson you will be able to design struct tags for predictable JSON, marshal and unmarshal reliably, and create composite keys that form lexicographic indexes for efficient range queries. Think about one query you will need often, because that query should guide how you model keys and attributes.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: This chapter gives you four concrete competencies. First, you will be able to represent nested application objects and serialize them for ledger storage, ensuring your Go structs map to predictable JSON forms. Second, you will understand and use Go struct tags so that fields map to the correct JSON names and optional fields are controlled. Third, you will learn to construct and use composite keys to index and query by multiple attributes, and iterate results safely. Fourth, you will adopt best practices for world state modeling that balance query efficiency and storage structure. Each objective includes a short how-and-why: for example, serializing with JSON ensures CouchDB can perform document queries in later chapters, and composite keys provide a LevelDB-friendly lexicographic index when rich queries are not available. These skills matter because poorly modeled state leads to slow queries and brittle chaincode. By practicing with the provided examples you will be able to implement and test patterns for production chaincode.

screens.title: JSON Marshaling and Unmarshaling
screens.narratorSegment: JSON marshaling is the controlled conversion of an in-memory Go struct into a JSON byte array suitable for ledger storage. Unmarshaling is the reverse: taking bytes from the world state and reconstructing the Go struct. In Fabric, world state stores values as byte arrays, so marshaling is mandatory for complex objects. A practical example is storing a Car asset with nested service records; you first convert the Car struct into a JSON byte array, then call the ledger storage operation. When reading the asset, you fetch the bytes and unmarshal them into your typed struct. Always check errors returned by both operations; marshaling can fail when a struct contains unsupported types or circular references, and unmarshaling fails when the stored JSON does not match your struct definitions or tags. Another common pitfall is relying on default field names: use struct tags to guarantee the JSON keys you expect. A misconception is to assume storing a struct directly will work; PutState requires bytes. Key takeaway: marshaling preserves structure for CouchDB queries, and careful error handling prevents runtime failures. Try the car example and confirm the fields round-trip correctly.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Marshaling converts structs to bytes for PutState; unmarshaling reconstructs typed structs from stored JSON bytes.

content.html:
Core Concept
JSON marshaling and unmarshaling
Why you must serialize complex objects before PutState and how to safely reconstruct them after GetState.
Key points
  • PutState stores byte arrays; convert structs to JSON bytes first.
  • Use the standard JSON library to marshal and unmarshal consistently.
  • Always check the error returned by marshal/unmarshal operations.
  • Struct tags control JSON field names and omissions for predictable storage.
Example: Car asset with nested service records that round-trip between struct and JSON.
Key Takeaway

Always marshal complex Go structs to JSON before PutState and validate on unmarshal.

Concrete example (visual)
A Car struct with a ServiceRecords slice becomes a single JSON document in world state, preserving nested arrays for later queries or client readout.
// Example struct (visualized) { "id": "CAR001", "make": "Toyota", "model": "Camry", "year": 2020, "owner": "Alice", "serviceRecords": [ {"date": "2023-01-15", "description": "Oil Change", "mileage": 5000} ] }

screens.title: Go Struct Tags and JSON Field Mapping
screens.narratorSegment: Struct tags are small annotations on your Go struct fields that determine how they serialize into JSON. They let you rename fields, omit empty values, and ensure the stored JSON matches A P I or query expectations. For example, labeling a field with a lowercased JSON name ensures clients and CouchDB queries see consistent keys. A frequent practical need is to ensure indexing attributes use specific names for composite keys or rich queries. Struct tags also help avoid accidental exposure of internal fields by omitting fields from JSON when needed. A common misconception is that field names automatically map correctly regardless of casing; in practice you must supply tags to guarantee stable JSON keys across code versions. When you change tags, remember that stored documents in world state may become inconsistent with new expectations; plan migrations or keep backward-compatible tags. Use tags sparingly and deliberately: they are part of your contract with clients and your query engine. After defining tags, test serialization and the resulting JSON keys before relying on them in composite key creation or CouchDB queries. Go Struct Tags and JSON Field Mapping means use json tags to enforce stable field names and optional omits; treat tags as part of your api and query contract.. In practical terms, control json output using struct tags. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Struct Tag Guidance
keyIdea.text: Use json tags to enforce stable field names and optional omits; treat tags as part of your API and query contract.

content.html:
Definition
Go struct tags: control JSON mapping
Tags guarantee the JSON keys produced by marshal, which affects client contracts and CouchDB queries.
  • Tags let you specify the serialized field name and include options like omit-empty.
  • Tags are the contract between your chaincode and any clients or query engines.
  • Changing tags without migration can cause unmarshalling mismatches for older records.
Common Mistake

Relying on Go field names without tags leads to unexpected JSON casing and failed queries. Always test the produced JSON.

Practical card: Field mapping
// Visualized mapping Field: Owner → JSON key: "owner" Field: ServiceRecords → JSON key: "serviceRecords" // Use tags to ensure these exact keys in stored documents
Why this matters
Query engines and clients read JSON keys. Tags make those keys predictable and stable across releases.

screens.title: Storing Complex Objects: PutState and GetState
screens.narratorSegment: Storing a nested asset involves a clear sequence of steps to preserve structure and avoid runtime errors. First, define a typed struct with appropriate JSON tags. Second, populate the struct and call the JSON marshal function to produce a byte array. Third, check the marshal result for errors; handle or return them to avoid silently storing invalid data. Fourth, choose a key: a primary key or a composite key depending on query needs. Fifth, call the ledger PutState operation with the key and byte array. When reading back, call GetState by the same key, check for a nil return which means the record does not exist, then unmarshal the returned bytes into your typed struct while checking for errors again. An important nuance is value semantics: unmarshal into a variable pointer so fields populate correctly. Also consider whether to store the full object under both a primary key and a composite index, remembering that duplication must be managed. This step-by-step approach prevents the common mistakes of sending malformed JSON, ignoring errors, or storing structs without serialization. Storing Complex Objects: PutState and GetState means define, marshal, verify errors, choose the key, and call putstate. on read, getstate, check nil, and unmarshal safely.. In practical terms, the sequence for safely saving and loading nested assets. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Safe storage process
keyIdea.text: Define, marshal, verify errors, choose the key, and call PutState. On read, GetState, check nil, and unmarshal safely.

content.html:
Process Flow
Saving and loading complex objects
1.
Define typed structs and JSON tags for stable serialization.
2.
Marshal to JSON byte array and check for errors before storing.
3.
Choose a key pattern: primary key or composite key for indexing.
4.
Call PutState with key and bytes. On read, use GetState, check nil, then unmarshal back into a struct pointer.
Concrete example card
Create a Car object, marshal it, store with the car ID. Retrieve by ID and unmarshal back to work with fields.
// Pseudocode sequence
carJSON, err := jsonMarshal(car)
if err != nil { return err }
err = stub.PutState(car.ID, carJSON)
// On read
bytes, err := stub.GetState(car.ID)
if bytes == nil { return notFound }
err = jsonUnmarshal(bytes, &car)
Pitfall

Do not skip error checks or assume GetState always returns bytes; handle nil and unmarshal errors explicitly.

keyIdea.title: Code focus
keyIdea.text: Define typed structs with JSON tags, populate nested slices, marshal to JSON, and check errors before PutState.

content.html:
Code Walkthrough
Struct definitions (visual)
type Car struct {
    ID string `json:"id"`
    Make string `json:"make"`
    Model string `json:"model"`
    Year int `json:"year"`
    Owner string `json:"owner"`
    ServiceRecords []ServiceRecord `json:"serviceRecords"`
}

type ServiceRecord struct {
    Date string `json:"date"`
    Description string `json:"description"`
    Mileage int `json:"mileage"`
}
Marshal and store
Populate a Car, marshal it with JSON, check error, then call PutState with the car ID and resulting bytes.
// Pseudocode
car := Car{ID: "CAR001", Make: "Toyota", ...}
carAsBytes, err := jsonMarshal(car)
if err != nil { return error }
err = stub.PutState(car.ID, carAsBytes)
if err != nil { return error }
Example result

Stored document preserves nested serviceRecords array for later reads and queries.

screens.title: Retrieving Data: GetState and Unmarshal
screens.narratorSegment: Reading a stored object reverses the marshal process. Use the ledger read operation to obtain the stored bytes. If the returned bytes are nil, the record is absent and you should return a clear error. Otherwise, unmarshal the bytes into a typed struct pointer so fields populate correctly. Handle errors from the unmarshal call: malformed JSON or mismatched tags can cause failures. After successful unmarshal, the struct contains the nested arrays and fields you defined earlier and you can operate on them in your chaincode logic. The chapter's example shows extracting the car ID from a composite key when iterating results; that is done by splitting the composite key into parts. Remember that GetState returns what you stored: if you stored the full object under a composite key value, the iterator's queryResponse includes the bytes you can unmarshal directly. Test reading both by primary ID and by composite-key iterator to ensure both paths yield identical structs after unmarshal. A misconception is assuming GetState always returns an error when a key is missing; instead it returns nil bytes and a nil error, so check the byte value explicitly.

keyIdea.title: Read reliably
keyIdea.text: Check for nil bytes from GetState, then unmarshal into a struct pointer and handle errors to avoid corrupt data handling.

content.html:
Code Walkthrough
GetState → unmarshal sequence
Check nil bytes, then unmarshal into your typed struct pointer to restore nested fields.
// Pseudocode
carAsBytes, err := stub.GetState(carID)
if err != nil { return err }
if carAsBytes == nil { return fmtError("does not exist") }
var car Car
err = jsonUnmarshal(carAsBytes, &car)
if err != nil { return err }
// Now car has fields and serviceRecords
Iterator case
When using a partial composite key query, iterate responses and unmarshal the Value from each record. Extract ID by splitting the composite key if you need the primary ID.
// Iteration pseudocode resultsIterator, _ := stub.GetStateByPartialCompositeKey(...) for resultsIterator.HasNext() { resp := resultsIterator.Next() _, parts, _ := splitCompositeKey(resp.Key) id := parts[len(parts)-1] var car Car jsonUnmarshal(resp.Value, &car) }

screens.title: Composite Keys: Building Indexes
screens.narratorSegment: Composite keys combine multiple attribute values into a single key string that sorts lexicographically in the world state. They are useful for creating secondary indexes when you need queries by attribute combinations, and especially valuable when rich CouchDB queries are not available. To create an index for cars by make and model, build a composite key that includes the make, model, and the asset ID as the final element; the ID as the last part ensures a unique key while allowing prefix queries on make and model. When you need all cars of a make and model, use a GetStateByPartialCompositeKey call with the make and model as the partial key. The world state returns an iterator of matching keys in sorted order. A common pitfall is choosing the wrong attribute order in the composite key for the query you need — remember composite key prefixing follows left-to-right lexicographic ordering. Also avoid over-indexing: creating composite keys for every possible query pattern leads to duplication and maintenance overhead. Design composite keys based on your most frequent queries, and prefer CouchDB rich queries only when available and necessary.

keyIdea.title: Indexing rule
keyIdea.text: Pick attribute order in composite keys to match query prefixes. Use partial-key queries to retrieve grouped records efficiently.

content.html:
Core Concept
Composite keys and lexicographic indexing
Compose attributes in the order you will query. The key order determines what partial queries are efficient.
Example index
Create a key like: indexName~Make~Model~ID so you can query by make and model together.
Common mistake
If you need to query by status then owner, put status first and owner second. Wrong order forces inefficient in-code filtering.
Key Takeaway

Design composite keys to match your query prefixes and avoid unnecessary duplication.

screens.title: CreateCompositeKey in Practice
screens.narratorSegment: Here we practice building a composite key for a Car or Product and storing the full object. Use the state context's CreateCompositeKey method with an index name and the ordered attributes you need in the index. The example uses an index name such as ProductByCategoryManufacturer and supplies category, manufacturer, and the product ID. Check for errors from the create call, then use PutState with either the composite key or additionally store the full object under a primary key. Storing the full object under the composite key value is common when you want the iterator to return both key and value in one step. Remember that composite keys themselves are just strings — the ledger does not enforce schema, so your application must be consistent about how it composes and later splits keys. When iterating over results, SplitCompositeKey returns the individual parts so you can recover the original ID. Avoid storing only an index with an empty value unless that pattern suits your read paths; storing the object as the value saves a second GetState call when iterating. CreateCompositeKey in Practice means create the composite key, check for errors, and decide whether to store the object as the composite key's value for easier iteration.. In practical terms, building and storing records using composite keys. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

CreateCompositeKey and PutState

Process Flow
GetStateByPartialCompositeKey and iteration
Fetch an iterator, loop through results, split composite keys to recover parts, unmarshal values into structs.
Iteration pseudocode
resultsIterator, err := stub.GetStateByPartialCompositeKey(indexName, []string{make, model})
defer resultsIterator.Close()
for resultsIterator.HasNext() {
  resp, _ := resultsIterator.Next()
  _, parts, _ := stub.SplitCompositeKey(resp.Key)
  id := parts[len(parts)-1]
  var car Car
  jsonUnmarshal(resp.Value, &car)
}
Practical tips
  • Defer closing iterators to avoid resource leaks.
  • Check Next errors and handle them to avoid silent failures.
  • Design composite key order to match your intended partial queries.

screens.title: Composite Keys vs CouchDB Rich Queries
screens.narratorSegment: There are two common ways to find records by attributes: composite keys and CouchDB rich queries. Composite keys are supported across state databases and provide a fast lexicographic index suitable for range queries and prefix matching. They are deterministic and simple, but they require careful design of attribute order and can result in duplicated values if you also store primary keys. CouchDB rich queries operate on JSON document fields and allow flexible query expressions, including logical operators and nested field queries, which can simplify some query needs. However, rich queries depend on CouchDB being enabled and can have different performance characteristics. The choice depends on deployment constraints and query patterns. If you require cross-database compatibility and predictable ordering, composite keys are safer. If you need complex ad-hoc filtering and CouchDB is available, rich queries offer more expressiveness. A misconception is to expect one approach to be universally superior; combine both patterns where appropriate and design data modeling to support your most frequent queries efficiently. Composite Keys vs CouchDB Rich Queries means use composite keys for portable, ordered indexes; use couchdb rich queries for flexible document queries when couchdb is available.. In practical terms, trade-offs when choosing an indexing strategy. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Comparison
Composite Keys
Portable, lexicographic, efficient for prefix and range queries. Requires planned attribute ordering.
  • Works with LevelDB and CouchDB.
  • Deterministic ordering for range scans.
  • May duplicate stored objects if also using primary keys.
Comparison
CouchDB Rich Queries
Flexible JSON queries, expressive filters, and nested field matching. Dependent on CouchDB and its indexing configuration.
  • Allows complex ad-hoc queries and logical operators.
  • Requires CouchDB and appropriate indexes for performance.
  • Less predictable ordering unless explicitly sorted.
Guideline

Model hybrid strategies: composite keys for common range queries and CouchDB for complex ad-hoc filtering when available.

fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter we focus on real-world ledger data: nested objects, arrays, and indexed relationships. You will learn how to convert Go application structs into JSON byte arrays for safe storage on the ledger, and how to build composite keys to query by multiple attributes. We will use concrete examples such as a Car asset with service records and a Product composed of multiple components. Understanding serialization and keying is important because Fabric stores state as byte arrays and your query patterns must be encoded into your data model. A common mistake is trying to store a Go struct directly or failing to check errors when marshalling and unmarshalling; we'll show safe patterns to avoid that. By the end of this lesson you will be able to design struct tags for predictable JSON, marshal and unmarshal reliably, and create composite keys that form lexicographic indexes for efficient range queries. Think about one query you will need often, because that query should guide how you model keys and attributes.

This chapter gives you four concrete competencies. First, you will be able to represent nested application objects and serialize them for ledger storage, ensuring your Go structs map to predictable JSON forms. Second, you will understand and use Go struct tags so that fields map to the correct JSON names and optional fields are controlled. Third, you will learn to construct and use composite keys to index and query by multiple attributes, and iterate results safely. Fourth, you will adopt best practices for world state modeling that balance query efficiency and storage structure. Each objective includes a short how-and-why: for example, serializing with JSON ensures CouchDB can perform document queries in later chapters, and composite keys provide a LevelDB-friendly lexicographic index when rich queries are not available. These skills matter because poorly modeled state leads to slow queries and brittle chaincode. By practicing with the provided examples you will be able to implement and test patterns for production chaincode.

You will practice these skills through examples and a hands-on activity. Start by defining Go structs for an asset such as a Car, with nested service records, then implement marshal and put state operations to store the serialized JSON. Next, create composite keys that reflect your query patterns, for example indexing by make and model, and use partial composite key queries to retrieve groups of records. Pay careful attention to error checks at each I-O boundary. The supplied Product chaincode exercise will guide you through initializing sample data, creating products with nested components, and querying by category and manufacturer using a composite key. Working through a live invoke and query will show how stored JSON and composite key indexes interact in the ledger. This applied practice reinforces the theory: correct serialization preserves structure, and correct key design enables efficient retrieval.

JSON marshaling is the controlled conversion of an in-memory Go struct into a JSON byte array suitable for ledger storage. Unmarshaling is the reverse: taking bytes from the world state and reconstructing the Go struct. In Fabric, world state stores values as byte arrays, so marshaling is mandatory for complex objects. A practical example is storing a Car asset with nested service records; you first convert the Car struct into a JSON byte array, then call the ledger storage operation. When reading the asset, you fetch the bytes and unmarshal them into your typed struct. Always check errors returned by both operations; marshaling can fail when a struct contains unsupported types or circular references, and unmarshaling fails when the stored JSON does not match your struct definitions or tags. Another common pitfall is relying on default field names: use struct tags to guarantee the JSON keys you expect. A misconception is to assume storing a struct directly will work; PutState requires bytes. Key takeaway: marshaling preserves structure for CouchDB queries, and careful error handling prevents runtime failures. Try the car example and confirm the fields round-trip correctly.

Struct tags are small annotations on your Go struct fields that determine how they serialize into JSON. They let you rename fields, omit empty values, and ensure the stored JSON matches A P I or query expectations. For example, labeling a field with a lowercased JSON name ensures clients and CouchDB queries see consistent keys. A frequent practical need is to ensure indexing attributes use specific names for composite keys or rich queries. Struct tags also help avoid accidental exposure of internal fields by omitting fields from JSON when needed. A common misconception is that field names automatically map correctly regardless of casing; in practice you must supply tags to guarantee stable JSON keys across code versions. When you change tags, remember that stored documents in world state may become inconsistent with new expectations; plan migrations or keep backward-compatible tags. Use tags sparingly and deliberately: they are part of your contract with clients and your query engine. After defining tags, test serialization and the resulting JSON keys before relying on them in composite key creation or CouchDB queries. Go Struct Tags and JSON Field Mapping means use json tags to enforce stable field names and optional omits; treat tags as part of your api and query contract.. In practical terms, control json output using struct tags. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Storing a nested asset involves a clear sequence of steps to preserve structure and avoid runtime errors. First, define a typed struct with appropriate JSON tags. Second, populate the struct and call the JSON marshal function to produce a byte array. Third, check the marshal result for errors; handle or return them to avoid silently storing invalid data. Fourth, choose a key: a primary key or a composite key depending on query needs. Fifth, call the ledger PutState operation with the key and byte array. When reading back, call GetState by the same key, check for a nil return which means the record does not exist, then unmarshal the returned bytes into your typed struct while checking for errors again. An important nuance is value semantics: unmarshal into a variable pointer so fields populate correctly. Also consider whether to store the full object under both a primary key and a composite index, remembering that duplication must be managed. This step-by-step approach prevents the common mistakes of sending malformed JSON, ignoring errors, or storing structs without serialization. Let's walk through the Car asset example. Start by declaring a Car struct with fields like an identifier, make, model, year, owner, and a slice of service records. Each ServiceRecord holds a date, description, and mileage. The struct tags define the JSON field names so that the stored document keys are consistent. Reading a stored object reverses the marshal process. Use the ledger read operation to obtain the stored bytes. If the returned bytes are nil, the record is absent and you should return a clear error. Otherwise, unmarshal the bytes into a typed struct pointer so fields populate correctly. Handle errors from the unmarshal call: malformed JSON or mismatched tags can cause failures. After successful unmarshal, the struct contains the nested arrays and fields you defined earlier and you can operate on them in your chaincode logic. The chapter's example shows extracting the car ID from a composite key when iterating results; that is done by splitting the composite key into parts. Remember that GetState returns what you stored: if you stored the full object under a composite key value, the iterator's queryResponse includes the bytes you can unmarshal directly. Test reading both by primary ID and by composite-key iterator to ensure both paths yield identical structs after unmarshal. A misconception is assuming GetState always returns an error when a key is missing; instead it returns nil bytes and a nil error, so check the byte value explicitly.

Composite keys combine multiple attribute values into a single key string that sorts lexicographically in the world state. They are useful for creating secondary indexes when you need queries by attribute combinations, and especially valuable when rich CouchDB queries are not available. To create an index for cars by make and model, build a composite key that includes the make, model, and the asset ID as the final element; the ID as the last part ensures a unique key while allowing prefix queries on make and model. Also avoid over-indexing: creating composite keys for every possible query pattern leads to duplication and maintenance overhead. Design composite keys based on your most frequent queries, and prefer CouchDB rich queries only when available and necessary.

When iterating over results, SplitCompositeKey returns the individual parts so you can recover the original ID.
